## Prerequisites

- None. This is the first story in the **Foundation & Administration** feature and establishes the authentication foundation that later stories (users management, roles & permissions, departments/branches, audit logs, system configuration) build on.
- The repository currently contains only `.squad/` planning metadata. No backend or frontend project exists yet; this story therefore also introduces the initial ASP.NET Core Web API solution and the React + TypeScript client under conventional folders.
- .NET SDK **10.x** and Node **20.19+** (Vite 7 requirement) must be installed.
- A reachable **SQL Server** instance. For local development the expected one is **SQL Server LocalDB** (`(localdb)\MSSQLLocalDB`), which ships with the Visual Studio *Data storage and processing* workload or the standalone *SQL Server Express LocalDB* installer. Verify with `sqllocaldb info MSSQLLocalDB`; start it with `sqllocaldb start MSSQLLocalDB`. A full SQL Server / Express instance or the `mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest` container works equally well — only `ConnectionStrings:Default` changes. Note LocalDB is **Windows-only**; on macOS/Linux use the container.
- Coordinate naming with the intake folders under `.squad/stories/foundation-and-administration/` so subsequent stories (`users-management`, `roles-permissions`, …) can plug into the same solution.

---

## Story Goal

Deliver a simple, secure authentication and login capability for the Customer Support CRM:

1. A CRM user can submit valid **email + password** credentials to a backend endpoint and receive a signed **JWT access token**.
2. Invalid credentials are rejected with an HTTP `401 Unauthorized` and a user-facing error message on the login screen.
3. Protected CRM API endpoints require a valid bearer token; unauthenticated requests receive `401`.
4. The React frontend exposes a **/login** screen, persists the token, attaches it to API calls, and redirects unauthenticated users away from protected routes.
5. Passwords are stored using **`PasswordHasher<TUser>`** from `Microsoft.Extensions.Identity.Core` (PBKDF2). Plaintext passwords are never logged, persisted, or returned in responses.

**Not in scope** (explicitly deferred to other stories in this feature): user CRUD/management UI and endpoints, roles & permissions enforcement beyond an `Authenticated` policy, departments/branches, audit logs, system configuration & branding, customer-portal auth, password reset, self-registration, MFA, and refresh tokens.

### 2 — Domain entity

**Create file:** `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Domain/Users/User.cs`

```csharp
namespace CustomerSupportCrm.Domain.Users;

public class User
{
    public Guid Id { get; set; } = Guid.NewGuid();
    public string Email { get; set; } = default!;      // stored lower-cased (invariant), unique
    public string DisplayName { get; set; } = default!;
    public string PasswordHash { get; set; } = default!;
    public bool IsActive { get; set; } = true;
    public DateTimeOffset CreatedAt { get; set; } = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;
}
```

#### User entity forward-compatibility

Story 02 (`users-management`) will extend this entity. This story must make that additive, and must **not** pre-build any of it:

- **Do not add** `UpdatedAt`, `RoleId`, `DepartmentId`, `BranchId`, `LastLoginAt`, soft-delete flags, or navigation properties now. Each is a one-column additive EF migration in the story that needs it, and adding them here would be scope creep with no consumer.
- The properties above are exactly what login requires; every one of them is also needed by Story 02, so none will need renaming or retyping.
- Guarantees that keep later stories non-breaking, and that this story must not violate:
  - `public` class in `CustomerSupportCrm.Domain` with a public parameterless constructor and settable properties — EF- and mapper-friendly, no `sealed`, no `record`, no private setters, no factory-only construction.
  - `Guid` surrogate key (not an auto-increment `int`) — safe to create rows from any layer without a DB round-trip.
  - No business rules baked into the entity. Validation lives in the API layer, so Story 02 can define its own create/update validation without fighting entity invariants.
  - Persistence config lives in `CrmDbContext.OnModelCreating` (or an `IEntityTypeConfiguration<User>`), not in attributes on the entity, so Story 02 can extend the mapping in one place.
- **Email normalization is a shared contract.** This story stores and queries `Email` as `value.Trim().ToLowerInvariant()`. Story 02 must apply the identical normalization on create/update or the unique index will let near-duplicates through. Put the normalization in one place — `static string Normalize(string email)` on a small `EmailNormalizer` helper in `Api/Auth/` (or `Domain/Users/`) — and document it with a comment saying later stories must reuse it. Do **not** rely on DB collation. SQL Server's default collation (`SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS`) is *case-insensitive*, which is actively dangerous here: it would silently mask a missing normalization in this story and then break the day someone deploys against a case-sensitive collation, or compares emails in C# with `StringComparison.Ordinal`. Normalize in application code so the behaviour is identical regardless of collation, and do **not** set an explicit collation on the `Email` column.

### 3 — Persistence

**Create files:**

- `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Infrastructure/Persistence/CrmDbContext.cs` — `DbSet<User> Users`; in `OnModelCreating` configure a unique index on `Email` and column lengths (`Email` 256, `DisplayName` 128, `PasswordHash` 512). All three are required (non-nullable). On SQL Server these map to `nvarchar(256)` / `nvarchar(128)` / `nvarchar(512)`; the lengths are **mandatory, not cosmetic** — an unbounded `nvarchar(max)` cannot participate in an index key at all, and SQL Server caps a nonclustered index key at 1700 bytes (900 on a clustered key, and 900 everywhere before SQL Server 2016). `nvarchar(256)` is 512 bytes, comfortably inside every one of those limits; anything above `nvarchar(450)` starts to risk them. Map `Id` as a plain `uniqueidentifier` with `ValueGeneratedNever()`: the application assigns the `Guid`, so do not let SQL Server default it with `NEWID()`/`NEWSEQUENTIALID()`.
- `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Infrastructure/Persistence/DbSeeder.cs` — if `Users` is empty, seed a **single** admin user from configuration section `AuthSettings:SeedAdmin` (`Email`, `Password`, `DisplayName`). Normalize the email, hash the password with `PasswordHasher<User>`, save. If the section is missing or incomplete, log a warning (see below) and return without throwing — the app must still start.

Seeding rules:

- Seeding runs in **`Development` only**, alongside the automatic migration. Production admin provisioning is out of scope for this story; `backend/README.md` documents that a production deployment must create the first user manually (e.g. `dotnet ef database update` then an INSERT with a hash produced by the same hasher) until Story 02 ships user management.
- Seeder is idempotent: it checks `await db.Users.AnyAsync()` and does nothing if any user exists. It never updates or resets an existing admin.

Migrations:

- Add an initial migration named `InitialCreate` under `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Infrastructure/Migrations/`:
  ```
  dotnet ef migrations add InitialCreate \
    --project backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Infrastructure \
    --startup-project backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api
  ```
- On startup, in `Development` only: `await db.Database.MigrateAsync();` then run the seeder. Use `MigrateAsync`, **never** `EnsureCreated` — `EnsureCreated` bypasses the migrations history table and would leave the dev DB unable to accept Story 02's migration.
- Wrap the startup migrate+seed in a scoped block (`app.Services.CreateScope()`) before `app.Run()`.

### 4 — Authentication configuration

**Create file:** `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api/Auth/JwtOptions.cs`

```csharp
namespace CustomerSupportCrm.Api.Auth;

public class JwtOptions
{
    public const string SectionName = "Jwt";

    public string Issuer { get; set; } = default!;
    public string Audience { get; set; } = default!;
    public string SigningKey { get; set; } = default!;   // >= 32 UTF-8 bytes (256-bit, HMAC-SHA256)
    public int AccessTokenMinutes { get; set; } = 60;
}
```

**Signing-key validation — fail fast at startup, not lazily.** Register with the options validation pipeline so a bad key stops the host before it serves a single request:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddOptions<JwtOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(JwtOptions.SectionName))
    .Validate(o => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(o.Issuer),   "Jwt:Issuer is required.")
    .Validate(o => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(o.Audience), "Jwt:Audience is required.")
    .Validate(o => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(o.SigningKey),
        "Jwt:SigningKey is required. Set it via environment variable Jwt__SigningKey, user-secrets, or a secrets manager.")
    .Validate(o => Encoding.UTF8.GetByteCount(o.SigningKey ?? string.Empty) >= 32,
        "Jwt:SigningKey must be at least 32 bytes (256 bits) for HMAC-SHA256.")
    .Validate(o => o.AccessTokenMinutes is > 0 and <= 24 * 60, "Jwt:AccessTokenMinutes must be between 1 and 1440.")
    .ValidateOnStart();
```

Notes:
- Measure the key in **UTF-8 bytes** (`Encoding.UTF8.GetByteCount`), not `string.Length` — a key of 32 non-ASCII characters is longer than 32 bytes, and length in chars is the wrong unit for a byte-oriented HMAC key.
- `ValidateOnStart()` throws `OptionsValidationException` during host startup. This replaces the previous plan's "validate in the `JwtTokenService` constructor", which would only surface on the first login attempt.
- The same validator covers both the empty-key case and the short-key case, in every environment. The previous plan's "fails fast if empty in non-Development" carve-out is gone: an empty key is invalid everywhere, and `appsettings.Development.json` supplies a valid dev key.

**Create file:** `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api/Auth/JwtTokenService.cs`

- Constructor takes `IOptions<JwtOptions>`. Register as a singleton.
- `AccessToken IssueAccessToken(User user)` returning `record AccessToken(string Token, DateTimeOffset ExpiresAt)` — the controller needs both, so returning them together avoids recomputing expiry.
- Claims (payload contract — see the forward-compatibility section below):
  | Claim | Value |
  |-------|-------|
  | `sub` | `user.Id` (`"D"` format) |
  | `email` | `user.Email` (normalized) |
  | `name` | `user.DisplayName` |
  | `iat`, `exp`, `nbf` | UTC, from `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` and `AccessTokenMinutes` |
  | `iss`, `aud` | from options |
  | `jti` | `Guid.NewGuid()` — gives the future audit-logs story a token correlation id at no cost |
- Sign with **HMAC-SHA256** over `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(SigningKey)` using `SymmetricSecurityKey` + `SigningCredentials(key, SecurityAlgorithms.HmacSha256)`.

#### JWT forward-compatibility contract (must be satisfied by this story)

The goal is that a future Roles & Permissions story can add authorization data **without a breaking change** to tokens, clients, or call sites. Three concrete requirements:

1. **`MapInboundClaims = false`** on the JWT bearer options. By default the inbound handler rewrites `sub` → `ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier` and `email` → `ClaimTypes.Email`, so `User.FindFirst("sub")` silently returns `null`. Turning mapping off keeps every claim readable under the exact name it was issued with — which is also what a later `permissions` claim will need.
2. **Declare the claim types now** in `TokenValidationParameters`:
   ```csharp
   NameClaimType = "name",
   RoleClaimType = "role",
   ```
   No `role` claim is issued in this story. Declaring `RoleClaimType` now means that when Story 03 starts issuing `role`, `[Authorize(Roles = "...")]` and `User.IsInRole(...)` work immediately, with zero changes to configuration or to already-deployed clients.
3. **Read `sub` through one helper, not inline.** Create `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api/Auth/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs` with `Guid? GetUserId(this ClaimsPrincipal principal)` (reads `"sub"`, `Guid.TryParse`). Every consumer uses it. Later stories add `GetRole()` / `GetPermissions()` beside it instead of scattering magic strings.

Additive-only rules to write as a comment in `JwtTokenService`:

- Claims may only be **added**. Never rename or repurpose `sub`, `email`, `name`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`.
- Planned additions, deliberately **not** implemented here: `role` (single string) and `permissions` (JSON array of strings). Both fit the existing token structure; neither requires a version field, so **do not** add a `ver`/`schema` claim speculatively.
- Consumers (backend and frontend) must ignore unknown claims and unknown response fields rather than validating a closed shape. The frontend `AuthUser` type must therefore not be used with a runtime "reject unknown keys" validator.
- The `LoginResponse.user` DTO follows the same additive rule: `{ id, email, displayName }` today; `role`/`permissions` may be added later. Do **not** add optional `role?`/`permissions?` fields now — an absent field and a `null` field are different contracts, and there is nothing to populate them with.

**Edit file:** `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api/Program.cs`

- Bind and validate `JwtOptions` as shown above.
- Register: `AddDbContext<CrmDbContext>` (**SQL Server**, connection string `ConnectionStrings:Default`), `JwtTokenService`, and the hasher:
  ```csharp
  builder.Services.AddDbContext<CrmDbContext>(o => o.UseSqlServer(
      builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default"),
      sql => sql.EnableRetryOnFailure()));                // transient-fault resilience; costs nothing against LocalDB

  builder.Services.AddOptions<PasswordHasherOptions>();   // PasswordHasher<T> requires IOptions<PasswordHasherOptions>
  builder.Services.AddSingleton<IPasswordHasher<User>, PasswordHasher<User>>();
  ```
  > Caveat to carry forward, not to act on now: `EnableRetryOnFailure` installs a retrying execution strategy, and EF Core throws `InvalidOperationException` if such a strategy meets a **user-initiated** transaction (`BeginTransaction`). Nothing in this story opens one — the single `SaveChangesAsync` on the rehash path is covered by EF's own transaction. A later story that needs an explicit transaction must wrap it in `db.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy().ExecuteAsync(...)`.
- `AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme).AddJwtBearer(options => { ... })` with:
  ```csharp
  options.MapInboundClaims = false;
  options.TokenValidationParameters = new TokenValidationParameters
  {
      ValidateIssuer = true,           ValidIssuer = jwt.Issuer,
      ValidateAudience = true,         ValidAudience = jwt.Audience,
      ValidateLifetime = true,
      ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true, IssuerSigningKey = new SymmetricSecurityKey(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(jwt.SigningKey)),
      ClockSkew = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30),   // tolerates modest server/client clock drift
      NameClaimType = "name",
      RoleClaimType = "role",                 // reserved for Story 03; no role claim is issued yet
  };
  ```
- `AddAuthorization()` with a **fallback policy** requiring an authenticated user, plus a named `"Authenticated"` policy for explicit use:
  ```csharp
  builder.Services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
      .SetFallbackPolicy(new AuthorizationPolicyBuilder().RequireAuthenticatedUser().Build())
      .AddPolicy("Authenticated", p => p.RequireAuthenticatedUser());
  ```
  Use `SetFallbackPolicy`, not `SetDefaultPolicy`. The fallback applies to endpoints with **no** authorization metadata (secure-by-default: a new controller added by a later story is protected unless it opts out with `[AllowAnonymous]`); the default policy only applies to endpoints already marked `[Authorize]` with no policy named. The login endpoint and the anonymous diagnostics endpoint must be marked `[AllowAnonymous]` explicitly.
- **Model-validation response shape.** ASP.NET Core's automatic `[ApiController]` 400 returns `ValidationProblemDetails`, which does **not** match the `{ "error": "invalid_request" }` contract this story's tests assert. Override it:
  ```csharp
  builder.Services.Configure<ApiBehaviorOptions>(o =>
      o.InvalidModelStateResponseFactory = _ => new BadRequestObjectResult(new { error = "invalid_request" }));
  ```
- **CORS.** Add policy `"Frontend"`, reading the origins from configuration so a deployment needs no code change:
  ```csharp
  var corsOrigins = builder.Configuration.GetSection("Cors:AllowedOrigins").Get<string[]>() ?? [];
  builder.Services.AddCors(o => o.AddPolicy("Frontend", p => p
      .WithOrigins(corsOrigins)
      .WithHeaders("Authorization", "Content-Type")
      .WithMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS")));
  ```
  The origins are **not** hard-coded: `appsettings.json` ships `"Cors": { "AllowedOrigins": [] }` and `appsettings.Development.json` supplies `http://localhost:5173`. An empty array means no cross-origin caller is allowed, which is the safe failure for a misconfigured deployment — do not add a hard-coded production fallback.
  **`AllowCredentials()` is removed.** This story authenticates with an `Authorization: Bearer` header, not cookies — nothing in the flow sends a cookie or a TLS client certificate, so credentialed CORS buys nothing and only widens what the browser is willing to expose cross-origin. Add `AllowCredentials()` only if a later story introduces cookie-based auth (e.g. refresh-token cookies), and note that doing so forbids wildcard origins.
  Also note in a comment: in local development the Vite proxy makes `/api` same-origin, so CORS is not exercised by the normal dev loop — it matters for a non-proxied client or a deployed frontend on a different host.
- Middleware order: `UseCors("Frontend")` → `UseAuthentication()` → `UseAuthorization()` → `MapControllers()`. `UseCors` must come first so `OPTIONS` preflights, which carry no `Authorization` header, are answered before authentication runs.
- **For integration testing:** with top-level statements, `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` cannot see `Program` unless it is public. Add at the end of `Program.cs`:
  ```csharp
  public partial class Program { }
  ```

### 5 — Endpoints

**Create file:** `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api/Auth/AuthController.cs`

```csharp
[ApiController]
[Route("api/auth")]
public class AuthController : ControllerBase
{
    // POST /api/auth/login  [AllowAnonymous]
    //   { email, password } => 200 { accessToken, expiresAt, user: { id, email, displayName } }
    // GET  /api/auth/me     [Authorize]
    //   => 200 { id, email, displayName }
}
```

DTOs live in `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api/Auth/Dtos.cs`:

```csharp
public record LoginRequest(
    [property: Required, EmailAddress, StringLength(256)] string Email,
    [property: Required, StringLength(256, MinimumLength = 1)] string Password);

public record UserDto(Guid Id, string Email, string DisplayName);
public record LoginResponse(string AccessToken, DateTimeOffset ExpiresAt, UserDto User);
```

`POST /api/auth/login` behaviour:

1. `[AllowAnonymous]`. Validate the model. Empty/whitespace/malformed email or empty password → `400 { "error": "invalid_request" }` (delivered by the `InvalidModelStateResponseFactory` above).
2. Normalize the email, look it up. If the user is not found **or** `IsActive == false` **or** password verification fails → `401 { "error": "invalid_credentials" }`. **Do not** distinguish the three cases in the response, the status code, or the timing-sensitive parts of the flow — that is what prevents account enumeration.
3. Verify with `IPasswordHasher<User>.VerifyHashedPassword`. On `PasswordVerificationResult.SuccessRehashNeeded`, re-hash the supplied password, assign it, and `SaveChangesAsync()` before issuing the token. This lets a later story raise the PBKDF2 iteration count without invalidating existing passwords.
4. On success, issue the token via `JwtTokenService` and return `accessToken`, `expiresAt` (UTC, ISO-8601), and the minimal `UserDto`. `PasswordHash` must never appear in any response — the DTO projection, not `[JsonIgnore]` on the entity, is what guarantees this.
5. Log via `ILogger<AuthController>` using message templates with named placeholders (never string interpolation):
   ```csharp
   _logger.LogInformation("event={Event} outcome={Outcome} userId={UserId} email={Email} remoteIp={RemoteIp}",
       "login", "success", user.Id, user.Email, HttpContext.Connection.RemoteIpAddress?.ToString());
   _logger.LogWarning("event={Event} outcome={Outcome} remoteIp={RemoteIp}",
       "login", "failure", HttpContext.Connection.RemoteIpAddress?.ToString());
   ```
   **Never** log the password, the raw token, or the password hash. On failure, `userId` and `email` are omitted (nothing is confirmed about whether the account exists).
   > Note for the audit-logs story, not for this one: brute-force detection normally wants the *attempted* email on failure too. That is a deliberate extension point, not an omission to fix here.

`GET /api/auth/me` behaviour:

1. `[Authorize]`. A missing, expired, malformed, or wrongly-signed token → `401` from the JWT bearer middleware (empty body — this is framework behaviour and is fine).
2. Read the id via `User.GetUserId()`. Then — **required, and the case the previous plan left undefined** — a token that is cryptographically valid but no longer corresponds to a usable account must also be rejected:
   - `GetUserId()` returns `null` (no `sub`, or unparseable) → `401 { "error": "unauthorized" }`
   - no user row with that id (deleted between issuance and use) → `401 { "error": "unauthorized" }`
   - user found but `IsActive == false` (deactivated after the token was issued) → `401 { "error": "unauthorized" }`
   Return `Unauthorized(new { error = "unauthorized" })` for all three; do not return `403`, `404`, or a `200` with a null body. This is what makes deactivation take effect within the token lifetime for the endpoint the frontend uses to establish its session, and it is what drives the frontend's automatic logout.
3. Otherwise return `200 { id, email, displayName }`.

**Create file:** `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api/Diagnostics/DiagnosticsController.cs`

```csharp
[ApiController]
[Route("api/diagnostics")]
public class DiagnosticsController : ControllerBase
{
    // GET /api/diagnostics/ping         [AllowAnonymous] => { status: "ok" }
    // GET /api/diagnostics/ping/secure  [Authorize]      => { status: "ok", userId: <sub> }
}
```

These are **smoke-test / diagnostics endpoints only — not CRM business functionality.** Consequences that this story must honour:

- They live under `api/diagnostics`, in a `Diagnostics/` folder, not at `api/ping` and not in a folder called `Sample`. The route name says what they are.
- Their only consumers are the manual verification steps and the integration tests in this story. **No frontend feature code calls them** — the previous plan had `HomePage` calling `/api/ping/secure` to "prove auth works", which would have wired a diagnostics endpoint into the product UI. The frontend proves authentication through `GET /api/auth/me`, which is the real contract.
- Add an XML doc comment on the controller stating that they exist to verify the auth pipeline end to end, carry no business data, and may be removed or moved behind a health-check gate once real protected endpoints exist in Story 02.
- Do not extend them with version info, DB status, uptime, or anything else. If a genuine health check is wanted later, that is `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.HealthChecks`, and it is not this story.

```json
{

  "Cors": { "AllowedOrigins": [] },

}
```

**Create file:** `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api/appsettings.Development.json`

```json
{
  "ConnectionStrings": { "Default": "Server=(localdb)\\MSSQLLocalDB;Database=CustomerSupportCrmDev;Trusted_Connection=True;MultipleActiveResultSets=True;TrustServerCertificate=True" },
  "Jwt": {
    "Issuer": "customer-support-crm",
    "Audience": "customer-support-crm-web",

    "AccessTokenMinutes": 60
  },
  "Cors": { "AllowedOrigins": [ "http://localhost:5173" ] },

    "SeedAdmin": { "Email": "admin@local.test", "Password": "Admin!23", "DisplayName": "Local Admin" }
  }

```

**Create file:** `backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api/Properties/launchSettings.json` — HTTP profile on `http://localhost:5080`, `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development`. The port must match the Vite proxy target.

**Seed email is `admin@local.test`, not `admin@local`.** Rationale, since this was raised explicitly: `LoginRequest.Email` carries `[EmailAddress]`, and .NET's `EmailAddressAttribute` is lenient enough that `admin@local` would in fact pass it (it checks for a single `@` that is neither first nor last character). The change is made anyway because a dotless domain is fragile in the surrounding layers — stricter validators, `<input type="email">` implementations, and any future SMTP or normalization step may reject or mangle it, and a seed credential that fails validation in one layer but not another is a confusing first-run failure. `.test` is reserved by **RFC 6761** for exactly this purpose: it can never be registered and never resolves, so it is unambiguous in logs and safe to commit. Use `admin@local.test` consistently in the seeder default, `appsettings.Development.json`, `backend/README.md`, the verification steps, and every test fixture.

**Create file:** `backend/README.md` — must document:
- Prerequisites (.NET 10 SDK, Node 20.19+, `dotnet-ef` 10.x, SQL Server LocalDB or another reachable SQL Server) and how to run — including `sqllocaldb start MSSQLLocalDB` as the first thing to check when startup fails with a `SqlException`.
- The dev database (`CustomerSupportCrmDev` on `(localdb)\MSSQLLocalDB`) and how to drop it for a clean slate.
- That the integration-test suite creates and drops its own LocalDB database per run, and that the `CRM_TEST_SQL` environment variable overrides that connection string on agents without LocalDB.
- The dev seed credentials `admin@local.test` / `Admin!23`, marked **local development only**, and that they must be rotated/removed before any shared environment.
- That production must supply `Jwt:SigningKey` via environment variable (`Jwt__SigningKey`) or a secrets manager — never `appsettings.json` — and that rotating it invalidates every outstanding token.
- That production must likewise supply `ConnectionStrings:Default` via `ConnectionStrings__Default` or a secrets manager, using a least-privilege SQL login (or a Managed Identity against Azure SQL) — never `sa`, never a committed connection string, and never `TrustServerCertificate=True` outside local development.
- That migrations are applied automatically **only** in `Development`; other environments run `dotnet ef database update` explicitly.
- Preferred local alternative to the committed dev key: `dotnet user-secrets set "Jwt:SigningKey" "<random 32+ bytes>"`.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
```

### 2 — Token storage (the module that breaks the axios ↔ context cycle)

**Create file:** `frontend/src/lib/tokenStorage.ts`

This is the single source of truth for the access token, and it is the design that resolves the circular-dependency problem. It imports **nothing** — not axios, not React — so it sits at the bottom of the dependency graph:

```
tokenStorage.ts  (no imports)
      ↑                    ↑
   http.ts              AuthContext.tsx
      ↑
  authApi.ts  ────────────→ (imported by AuthContext)
```

`http.ts → tokenStorage`, `AuthContext → tokenStorage`, `AuthContext → authApi → http`. Acyclic, with no `registerTokenProvider()` back-channel, no module-level mutable callback injected from React, and no `window` CustomEvent bus. The previous plan's "small `getToken()` provider registered by `AuthContext`" plus "dispatches a `logout` event" is replaced by this.

API:

```ts
const STORAGE_KEY = "crm.auth.token";
type Listener = (token: string | null) => void;

export function getToken(): string | null;
export function setToken(token: string): void;      // memory + localStorage + notify
export function clearToken(): void;                 // memory + localStorage + notify
export function subscribe(listener: Listener): () => void;   // returns unsubscribe
```

Implementation requirements:

- Hold the token in a module-level variable, initialized once from `localStorage`. Reads go to memory, so a `localStorage` failure degrades to memory-only rather than breaking auth.
- Every `localStorage` access is wrapped in `try/catch`. In private-browsing modes, quota-exceeded conditions, or any environment where storage access throws, the token lives in memory only: the user stays logged in for the session and is logged out on reload. Never let a storage error propagate into a render or a request.
- `setToken` / `clearToken` notify all subscribers synchronously after updating state.
- Register a `window.addEventListener("storage", ...)` handler at module scope that reacts to changes to `STORAGE_KEY` from another tab by updating the in-memory value and notifying subscribers. This gives **cross-tab logout synchronization** for free and is why the listener does not belong in `AuthContext`.
- Guard the `window`/`localStorage` access so the module is importable in a non-DOM context (`typeof window === "undefined"`).

### 3 — Shared HTTP client

**Create file:** `frontend/src/lib/http.ts`

- Export a preconfigured axios instance with `baseURL: "/api"`.
- **Request interceptor:** read `getToken()` from `tokenStorage`; if present, set `config.headers.Authorization = \`Bearer ${token}\``. Reading at request time (not at instance creation) means a login mid-session is picked up without rebuilding the client.
- **Response interceptor:** on a `401` response, call `clearToken()` and re-reject the error. `tokenStorage`'s subscribers do the rest — `AuthContext` drops the user, `ProtectedRoute` redirects. Do **not** retry, do **not** call a refresh endpoint (refresh tokens are out of scope), and do **not** navigate from inside the interceptor (routing belongs to React, and an imperative redirect here would need the router instance, reintroducing a cycle).
- **Exempt the login request from the 401 clear.** A `401` from `POST /api/auth/login` means "wrong password", not "session expired"; clearing the token there would fire a spurious logout notification while the user is already unauthenticated. Skip the clear when the failing request's URL is the login path.

### 4 — Auth module

**Create files under** `frontend/src/features/auth/`:

**`types.ts`**
```ts
export interface AuthUser { id: string; email: string; displayName: string; }
export interface LoginRequest { email: string; password: string; }
export interface LoginResponse { accessToken: string; expiresAt: string; user: AuthUser; }
```
Mirror the backend DTOs exactly (camelCase — the default `System.Text.Json` policy). Per the additive contract, treat these as open shapes: do not add speculative `role`/`permissions` fields, and do not validate responses against a closed schema that would reject the extra claims a later story adds.

**`authApi.ts`** — the **only** module that talks to the auth endpoints:
```ts
export async function login(req: LoginRequest): Promise<LoginResponse>;              // POST /auth/login
export async function me(config?: { signal?: AbortSignal }): Promise<AuthUser>;      // GET  /auth/me
```
Uses the shared `http` instance (`baseURL` is already `/api`, so paths are `/auth/login`, `/auth/me`). No token handling here — the interceptor owns that.

**`AuthContext.tsx`** — exposes:
```ts
interface AuthState {
  user: AuthUser | null;
  status: "loading" | "authenticated" | "anonymous";
  login(email: string, password: string): Promise<void>;
  logout(): void;
}
```

Requirements:

- **`status` is required, not optional.** On a page refresh the provider must first verify the stored token with `me()`, and during that window it is neither authenticated nor anonymous. Without a `loading` state, `ProtectedRoute` sees `user === null` on the first render and bounces a legitimately logged-in user to `/login` on every refresh. Render nothing (or a minimal placeholder) while `status === "loading"`.
- **Hydration effect,** on mount: if `getToken()` is `null`, go straight to `"anonymous"` and make no request. Otherwise call `me()`; on success set the user and `"authenticated"`; on failure set `"anonymous"` (the interceptor has already cleared the token on a `401`).
- **The hydration effect must be idempotent.** React 19 in StrictMode intentionally mounts, unmounts, and remounts effects in development, so a naive effect calls `me()` twice. Create an `AbortController`, pass `signal` to `me()`, and abort it in the cleanup function; ignore abort errors (`axios.isCancel`). Dev-only symptom, but it is exactly the kind of double-call this story must not ship.
- **Subscribe to `tokenStorage`** in a second effect: when the token becomes `null` (interceptor 401, another tab logging out, explicit logout), set `user = null` and `status = "anonymous"`. Return the unsubscribe function.
- **`login(email, password)`** is the single place the login request happens:
  ```ts
  const res = await authApi.login({ email, password });
  setToken(res.accessToken);       // tokenStorage: memory + localStorage + notify
  setUser(res.user);               // no second round-trip: the response already carries the user
  setStatus("authenticated");
  ```
  It **rethrows** on failure so `LoginPage` can render the error. It must not call `me()` afterwards — `LoginResponse.user` is exactly the same projection `me()` returns, and calling both would be the duplicate request this story is required to avoid.
- **`logout()`** calls `clearToken()`; the subscription handles the state reset, so `logout` does not set state directly (one code path for every way a session ends). No server call — there is no server-side session or token revocation list in this story.
- Use `createContext` + a provider component and a `useAuth` hook. React 19 allows `<AuthContext value={...}>` without `.Provider`; either form is fine, but be consistent.

**Exactly one login round-trip.** The required chain, with no other component allowed to call `authApi.login`:

```
LoginPage (submit)  →  useAuth().login(email, password)  →  authApi.login()  →  POST /api/auth/login
                                                          ↓
                                        setToken() + setUser() from the same response
```

`LoginPage` must not import `authApi` at all — that import is what would let a second call creep in. Enforce it in review, and the "one POST per submit" test below is what catches a regression.

**`useAuth.ts`** — thin hook over the context that throws a clear error when used outside the provider (satisfies strict null checks at every call site without optional chaining).

**`LoginPage.tsx`**

- Controlled `email` (`type="email"`) and `password` (`type="password"`) inputs with associated `<label>`s, inside a `<form onSubmit>`; submit via a `type="submit"` button so Enter works.
- Inline error region with `role="alert"`, rendered only when there is an error.
- Error mapping: `401` → `"Invalid email or password."`; anything else (network failure, `500`, `400`) → `"Something went wrong. Please try again."` Narrow with `axios.isAxiosError(err)` and read `err.response?.status`. Never surface the raw server error to the user.
- Disable the submit button while a request is in flight (`submitting` state) **and** when either field is empty after trimming. Reset `submitting` in a `finally` block so a failed attempt does not lock the form.
- Guard against double submission (fast double-click / Enter twice) by returning early when `submitting` is true — the second half of "login must not happen twice".
- On success: `await login(email, password)`, then navigate to the preserved intended path, or `/`:
  ```ts
  const from = (location.state as { from?: string } | null)?.from ?? "/";
  navigate(from, { replace: true });
  ```
  `replace: true` keeps `/login` out of the history stack. Note `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`/`strict` require the null-safe read shown.
- If `status === "authenticated"` when the page mounts (user navigates to `/login` while already logged in), redirect to `/` instead of showing the form.

**`ProtectedRoute.tsx`**

- Reads `status` from `useAuth()`.
- `"loading"` → render a placeholder; **do not redirect** (see the `status` rationale above).
- `"anonymous"` → `<Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from: location.pathname + location.search }} />`.
- `"authenticated"` → render `children` / `<Outlet />`.

### 5 — Routing

**Edit file:** `frontend/src/App.tsx`

- `<AuthProvider>` wraps `<BrowserRouter>` (so the provider is not remounted by navigation).
- Routes:
  - `/login` → `LoginPage` (public).
  - `/` → `ProtectedRoute` wrapping `HomePage`.
  - `*` → `<Navigate to="/" replace />`.
- `HomePage` (`frontend/src/features/home/HomePage.tsx`) renders `Welcome, {user.displayName}` plus a **Log out** button calling `logout()`. It makes **no API call of its own** — the user comes from `AuthContext`, which was populated either by the login response or by the `me()` hydration. It must not call the diagnostics ping endpoint.

### 6 — Styling

One minimal CSS module for the login form (`LoginPage.module.css`) and a small global reset. No design system, no theming, no CSS framework — Story 06 (system configuration & branding) owns that layer, and anything added here would have to be undone.

## Edge Cases & Failure Modes

| Case | Behaviour | Enforced in |
|------|-----------|-------------|
| Empty email or password submitted | Frontend disables submit while either field is blank; backend still returns `400 { error: "invalid_request" }` | `LoginPage.tsx` form state; `ApiBehaviorOptions.InvalidModelStateResponseFactory` |
| Malformed email submitted | `400 { error: "invalid_request" }` from `[EmailAddress]` | `LoginRequest` |
| Unknown email / wrong password / inactive user | All three return an identical `401 { error: "invalid_credentials" }` — no enumeration signal in status, body, or headers | `AuthController.Login` |
| **Valid token, user row deleted** | `401 { error: "unauthorized" }` | `AuthController.Me` |
| **Valid token, user deactivated after issuance** | `401 { error: "unauthorized" }`; frontend interceptor clears the token and the user lands on `/login` | `AuthController.Me` + `http.ts` |
| Token missing `sub`, or `sub` not a Guid | `401 { error: "unauthorized" }` | `ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.GetUserId` + `AuthController.Me` |
| Signing key missing or under 32 bytes | Host fails to start with `OptionsValidationException` naming the setting | `AddOptions<JwtOptions>().Validate(...).ValidateOnStart()` |
| Expired token on a protected call | Middleware `401`; interceptor clears token; `ProtectedRoute` redirects to `/login` | JWT bearer + `http.ts` + `tokenStorage` subscription |
| Tampered token / bad signature | Same as expiry | as above |
| `sub`/`email` claims unreadable after middleware mapping | Prevented by `MapInboundClaims = false` | `Program.cs` |
| Clock skew between server and client | `ClockSkew = 30s` on validation; `nbf`/`iat` issued in UTC | `Program.cs`, `JwtTokenService` |
| `localStorage` unavailable or throwing | Caught; token is memory-only for the session; user is logged out on reload | `tokenStorage.ts` |
| Two tabs, one logs out | `storage` event updates the module state and notifies subscribers; both tabs drop to `/login` | `tokenStorage.ts` |
| React 19 StrictMode double-invoking the hydration effect | `AbortController` in the effect cleanup; aborts ignored — exactly one effective `me()` call | `AuthContext.tsx` |
| Double-click / double Enter on submit | Early return while `submitting`; button disabled — one `POST /api/auth/login` per submit | `LoginPage.tsx` |
| `401` from the login request itself | Interceptor skips the token clear for the login path (nothing to clear; avoids a spurious logout notification) | `http.ts` |
| Password hash needs upgrading | `SuccessRehashNeeded` → re-hash and persist before issuing the token | `AuthController.Login` |
| CORS preflight | `OPTIONS` succeeds without auth because `UseCors` precedes `UseAuthentication`; no `AllowCredentials` is needed for header-based bearer auth | `Program.cs` |
| Unicode in email / display name | `Email` normalized with `Trim().ToLowerInvariant()` on both write and read paths; `DisplayName` preserved verbatim; columns are `nvarchar(256)` / `nvarchar(128)` — never `varchar`, which would mangle non-Latin display names | `EmailNormalizer`, `CrmDbContext` |
| Two emails differing only by case or surrounding whitespace | Normalization + unique index reject the duplicate; the same normalizer must be reused by Story 02 | `EmailNormalizer`, unique index |
| Dev database dropped between runs | `MigrateAsync` recreates the schema and the seeder recreates the admin on next Development startup | startup block, `DbSeeder` |
| SQL Server unreachable at startup | `MigrateAsync` throws and the app fails fast with the `SqlException` — the right behaviour, since a CRM with no database has nothing to serve. `EnableRetryOnFailure` covers transient drops at request time, **not** a stopped instance; `backend/README.md` names `sqllocaldb start MSSQLLocalDB` as the first check | startup block, `Program.cs` |
| `AuthSettings:SeedAdmin` missing or incomplete | App starts; seeder logs `"No seed admin configured; login is unavailable."` and returns without throwing | `DbSeeder` |
| A later story adds a controller and forgets `[Authorize]` | Fallback policy denies anonymous access by default | `SetFallbackPolicy` |

## Test Plan

### Backend — `backend/tests/CustomerSupportCrm.Api.Tests/`

**1. `Auth/JwtTokenServiceTests.cs` (unit)**
- Issues a token containing `sub`, `email`, `name`, `jti`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `iat`, `nbf`.
- `sub` round-trips as the user's `Guid`.
- `ExpiresAt` is `AccessTokenMinutes` after now (assert with tolerance).
- The issued token validates against the same key/issuer/audience, and **fails** validation against a different signing key.
- No claim contains the password or the password hash.

**2. `Auth/JwtOptionsValidationTests.cs` (unit)**
- Options validation **fails** when `SigningKey` is empty, and when it is shorter than 32 UTF-8 bytes; the failure message names `Jwt:SigningKey`.
- Validation **fails** for missing `Issuer` / `Audience`, and for `AccessTokenMinutes <= 0`.
- Validation **passes** for a compliant configuration.
- A 32-character multi-byte key passes while a 31-byte ASCII key fails, proving the check counts bytes rather than characters.
- (This replaces "throws when the key is short" from `JwtTokenServiceTests` — validation now lives in the options pipeline, not the service constructor.)

**3. `Auth/PasswordHashingTests.cs` (unit)**
- Hash/verify round-trip returns `Success`.
- Wrong password returns `Failed`.
- Two hashes of the same password differ (per-hash salt).
- The `SuccessRehashNeeded` path re-hashes and persists, and the user can still log in afterwards. If the hasher cannot be coerced into returning `SuccessRehashNeeded` directly, drive the controller branch with a fake `IPasswordHasher<User>` — the branch must be covered, not skipped.

**4. `Auth/AuthControllerTests.cs` (integration, `WebApplicationFactory<Program>`)**

Fixture requirements — these determine whether the suite works at all:
- Run against a **real SQL Server LocalDB database, created fresh per test run**. SQL Server has no in-memory equivalent of SQLite's `:memory:`, and `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.InMemory` must **not** be substituted: it has no relational semantics, so it would not exercise the `InitialCreate` migration, the unique index on `Email`, or the column-length constraints — three of the things this suite exists to prove.
- Give each fixture a unique database name so parallel test classes, and leftovers from a crashed run, cannot collide. Build it once in the fixture's field initializer — note the C# escaping, since `(localdb)\MSSQLLocalDB` contains a backslash:
  ```csharp
  private readonly string _connectionString =
      Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("CRM_TEST_SQL")
      ?? $@"Server=(localdb)\MSSQLLocalDB;Database=CrmAuthTests_{Guid.NewGuid():N};Trusted_Connection=True;TrustServerCertificate=True";
  ```
  Reading `CRM_TEST_SQL` first lets a CI agent without LocalDB point the suite at a SQL Server container. When it is set, append the unique database name to it rather than reusing one shared database.
- **Override the environment:** call `builder.UseEnvironment("Testing")` in `ConfigureWebHost`. Without this the test host inherits `Development` (and loads the Api's `appsettings.Development.json` from its content root), so the app's own startup block would migrate **and run `DbSeeder`**, quietly inserting `admin@local.test` into every test database. The fixture must be the only thing that creates data.
- **Separate registration from migration — they happen at different times.** In `ConfigureTestServices` you may only *register* services: remove the app's `DbContextOptions<CrmDbContext>` registration and re-add `UseSqlServer(_connectionString)`. There is no built service provider inside that callback, so `Migrate()` cannot be called there. Migrate afterwards, in `InitializeAsync`, once the host exists:
  ```csharp
  public async ValueTask InitializeAsync()
  {
      using var scope = Services.CreateScope();
      var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<CrmDbContext>();
      await db.Database.MigrateAsync();      // the real InitialCreate migration, not EnsureCreated
      await SeedTestUsersAsync(db);
  }
  ```
- `DisposeAsync` calls `db.Database.EnsureDeletedAsync()` inside a `try`/`finally` that still disposes the host, so the test database is dropped even when tests fail. Databases must not accumulate in the LocalDB instance across runs.
- Share one fixture per test class via `IClassFixture<T>` — creating and migrating a LocalDB database per test *method* is slow enough to matter. Keep the cases independent by having each seed the users it needs under distinct emails, rather than by resetting the database between tests.
- Supply `Jwt:*` values via `ConfigureAppConfiguration` with an in-memory collection so the suite does not depend on any `appsettings.*.json`. Supply `ConnectionStrings:Default` the same way, so the connection string is right even for anything resolved before `ConfigureTestServices` is applied.
- Seed test users directly through the context with hashes from the real `PasswordHasher<User>`.

Cases:
- `POST /auth/login`, valid credentials → `200`; body has `accessToken`, `expiresAt`, `user.{id,email,displayName}`; the raw response JSON contains **no** `passwordHash` (assert case-insensitively on the raw string, not just the deserialized DTO); the token parses as a JWT with the expected `sub`.
- Valid credentials with different casing / surrounding whitespace in the email → `200` (normalization works end to end).
- Wrong password → `401`, body exactly `{"error":"invalid_credentials"}`.
- Unknown email → `401`, byte-identical body to the wrong-password case.
- Inactive user, correct password → `401`, byte-identical body to the two cases above.
- Empty body, missing password, and malformed email → `400 { "error": "invalid_request" }` (this is the test that fails without the `InvalidModelStateResponseFactory` override).
- `GET /auth/me` with no token → `401`. With a valid token → `200` and the current user.
- `GET /auth/me` with a token signed by a **different** key → `401`.
- `GET /auth/me` with an **expired** token → `401` (issue one with a negative lifetime via a test-configured `AccessTokenMinutes` or a directly-constructed token).
- **`GET /auth/me` with a valid token whose user row was deleted → `401 { "error": "unauthorized" }`.**
- **`GET /auth/me` with a valid token whose user was deactivated after issuance → `401 { "error": "unauthorized" }`.**
- `GET /auth/me` with a valid token containing a non-Guid `sub` → `401 { "error": "unauthorized" }`.
- `GET /api/diagnostics/ping` anonymous → `200 { status: "ok" }`.
- `GET /api/diagnostics/ping/secure` without a token → `401`; with a valid token → `200` and the caller's id.
- **Fallback-policy check:** the anonymous diagnostics ping is reachable while `ping/secure` is not, confirming the fallback policy is applied and `[AllowAnonymous]` opts out correctly.
- No test asserts a `role` or `permissions` claim — none is issued in this story.

### Frontend — Vitest + Testing Library

**5. `frontend/src/features/auth/__tests__/LoginPage.test.tsx`**
- Renders labelled email and password inputs and a submit button.
- Submit is disabled while either field is empty.
- Shows `"Invalid email or password."` when the API returns `401` (mock `authApi.login` to reject with an axios-shaped `401`), inside a `role="alert"` region.
- Shows `"Something went wrong. Please try again."` on a `500` and on a network error.
- Submit is disabled while the request is pending and re-enabled after a failure.
- On success, navigates to `/`.
- Navigates to the path preserved in `location.state.from` when present.
- **Calls the login API exactly once per submit** — assert `authApi.login` (or the mocked adapter) has been called once, including under a rapid double-click. This is the regression guard for the duplicate-login requirement.
- `LoginPage` does not import `authApi` directly — it goes through `useAuth().login`.

**6. `frontend/src/features/auth/__tests__/AuthContext.test.tsx`**
- With no stored token, settles to `"anonymous"` and never calls `me()`.
- With a stored token, calls `me()` **once** and settles to `"authenticated"` with the returned user (render inside `<StrictMode>` so React 19's double-invoked effect is actually exercised — this is the assertion that catches the double request).
- With a stored token that `me()` rejects with `401`, settles to `"anonymous"` and the token is cleared.
- `login()` performs exactly one `POST` and does **not** additionally call `me()`.
- `logout()` clears the token and returns to `"anonymous"`.
- A `tokenStorage` change to `null` from outside (simulating another tab or the interceptor) drops the user to `"anonymous"`.

**7. `frontend/src/features/auth/__tests__/ProtectedRoute.test.tsx`**
- Renders children when authenticated.
- Redirects to `/login` when anonymous, preserving the intended path in `location.state.from`.
- While `status === "loading"`, renders neither the children nor a redirect — the refresh-bounce regression test.

**8. `frontend/src/lib/__tests__/http.test.ts`**
- Request interceptor attaches `Authorization: Bearer <token>` when a token is present, and omits the header when it is not.
- Response interceptor clears the stored token on `401` and notifies subscribers.
- Response interceptor does **not** clear the token on a `401` from the login path.
- Response interceptor leaves the token intact on `400` / `403` / `500`.
- The rejection is propagated (no swallowing, no retry).

**9. `frontend/src/lib/__tests__/tokenStorage.test.ts`**
- `setToken` / `getToken` / `clearToken` round-trip through memory and `localStorage`.
- Subscribers are notified on set and clear; unsubscribe stops notifications.
- When `localStorage.setItem` throws, `setToken` does not throw and `getToken` still returns the value from memory.
- A `storage` event for `crm.auth.token` from another tab updates the value and notifies subscribers.

**10. Typecheck:** `pnpm typecheck` (`tsc --noEmit`) passes with the strict config. Counted as part of the frontend suite.

## Migration / Rollback

- **Forward:** running the Api in `Development` applies `InitialCreate` via `MigrateAsync` and seeds the admin user. In every other environment, run
  ```
  dotnet ef database update --project backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Infrastructure \
                            --startup-project backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api
  ```
  before starting the app; no automatic migration and no seeding runs there.
- **Rollback:** `dotnet ef database update 0 --project ... --startup-project ...` drops the `Users` table. For a clean dev slate, stop the app and drop the database entirely — `dotnet ef database drop --force --project backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Infrastructure --startup-project backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api`, or `sqlcmd -S "(localdb)\MSSQLLocalDB" -Q "DROP DATABASE CustomerSupportCrmDev"` — and the next Development start recreates and reseeds it.
- **Half-applied state:** if the migration succeeds but seeding does not (missing `AuthSettings:SeedAdmin`), the app still starts and nobody can log in. The seeder logs `"No seed admin configured; login is unavailable."` at warning level so the cause is obvious in the first lines of output.
- **Story 02 compatibility:** because the schema is created by a real migration (not `EnsureCreated`), Story 02 can add its columns with a second migration. Never squash or edit `InitialCreate` after it has been applied anywhere.
- **Signing-key rotation:** rotating `Jwt:SigningKey` invalidates every outstanding token; all users must log in again. There is no refresh-token or dual-key grace window in this story — announce rotations before deploying.
- **Nothing to roll back on the frontend** beyond reverting the build; the only persisted client state is the `crm.auth.token` `localStorage` key, which is cleared by a `401` or by logging out.

## Verification Steps

1. **Toolchain:** `dotnet --version` reports **10.x**; `node --version` reports **20.19+**; `dotnet ef --version` reports **10.x**; `sqllocaldb info MSSQLLocalDB` shows the instance as **Running** (`sqllocaldb start MSSQLLocalDB` if it is not).
2. **Backend builds:** `dotnet build backend/CustomerSupportCrm.sln` — 0 errors, no new warnings in auth code.
3. **TFM check:** every `.csproj` resolves to `net10.0` (via `Directory.Build.props`); no `net8.0` or `net9.0` anywhere; no `8.0.*` or `9.0.*` package versions in the solution.
4. **Backend tests:** `dotnet test backend/tests/CustomerSupportCrm.Api.Tests/CustomerSupportCrm.Api.Tests.csproj` — all green.
5. **Fail-fast check:** temporarily set `Jwt__SigningKey=short` and run the Api — startup fails with a message naming `Jwt:SigningKey`. Restore the value afterwards.
6. **Backend runs:** `dotnet run --project backend/src/CustomerSupportCrm.Api` starts on `http://localhost:5080`; migration and seed complete without errors. Confirm the database exists — `sqlcmd -S "(localdb)\MSSQLLocalDB" -Q "SELECT name FROM sys.databases WHERE name = 'CustomerSupportCrmDev'"` returns one row, and `sqlcmd -S "(localdb)\MSSQLLocalDB" -d CustomerSupportCrmDev -Q "SELECT Email, IsActive FROM Users"` shows the seeded admin.
7. **Manual API check.** These are POSIX-shell commands — run them in Git Bash or WSL. In PowerShell, `curl` is an alias for `Invoke-WebRequest`, and single-quoted JSON is not passed through: use `curl.exe` with the bodies double-quoted and the inner quotes escaped, or `Invoke-RestMethod`.
   ```
   curl -i -X POST http://localhost:5080/api/auth/login \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{"email":"admin@local.test","password":"Admin!23"}'          # 200 + accessToken
   curl -i -X POST http://localhost:5080/api/auth/login \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{"email":"admin@local.test","password":"wrong"}'             # 401 {"error":"invalid_credentials"}
   curl -i -X POST http://localhost:5080/api/auth/login \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}'                     # 400 {"error":"invalid_request"}
   curl -i http://localhost:5080/api/diagnostics/ping                    # 200 {"status":"ok"}
   curl -i http://localhost:5080/api/diagnostics/ping/secure             # 401
   curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
        http://localhost:5080/api/diagnostics/ping/secure                # 200
   curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
        http://localhost:5080/api/auth/me                                # 200 {id,email,displayName}
   ```
8. **Deactivation check:** with a valid token in hand, deactivate the seeded admin — `sqlcmd -S "(localdb)\MSSQLLocalDB" -d CustomerSupportCrmDev -Q "UPDATE Users SET IsActive = 0 WHERE Email = 'admin@local.test'"` — then call `GET /api/auth/me` with that same token → `401 {"error":"unauthorized"}`. Restore it afterwards with `SET IsActive = 1`.
9. **Frontend installs and runs:** `pnpm install && pnpm dev` in `frontend/` starts Vite on `http://localhost:5173`; `pnpm why react` shows a single React **19** copy.
10. **Frontend typecheck + tests:** `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm test` are both green.
11. **End-to-end smoke:** open `http://localhost:5173/`, get redirected to `/login`, log in as `admin@local.test` / `Admin!23`, land on the home page showing `Welcome, Local Admin`.
12. **Duplicate-request check (the key manual check for the single-login requirement):** with the network tab open, submit the login form once — there must be **exactly one** `POST /api/auth/login` and **no** follow-up `GET /api/auth/me`. Then reload the page — exactly **one** `GET /api/auth/me` and no redirect to `/login`.
13. **Session-expiry check:** clear `crm.auth.token` from `localStorage` in devtools and reload — the user lands on `/login`. Then log in, corrupt the stored token, and trigger a request — the `401` clears the token and returns the user to `/login`.
14. **Cross-tab check:** log in, open a second tab on `/`, log out in the first — the second tab drops to `/login` on its next render.
15. **Deep-link check:** while logged out, visit `http://localhost:5173/some/protected/path` — redirected to `/login`; after logging in, land back on that path.
16. **Scope check:** the diff contains no user-management endpoints or UI, no roles/permissions, no departments/branches, no audit-log sink, no branding, no password reset, no registration, no MFA, no refresh tokens.

## Done Criteria

- [ ] Every project targets **`net10.0`**; no `net8.0`/`net9.0` TFMs and no `8.0.*`/`9.0.*` packages remain.
- [ ] Frontend runs on **React 19** with **Vite 7**, `strict: true` in `tsconfig.json`, and `tsc --noEmit` clean with no `any` and no error-silencing casts.
- [ ] Users can log in with valid credentials via `POST /api/auth/login` and receive a signed JWT.
- [ ] Invalid credentials return `401 { "error": "invalid_credentials" }` — identically for unknown email, wrong password, and inactive user — and the login screen shows `"Invalid email or password."`.
- [ ] `GET /api/auth/me` returns `401 { "error": "unauthorized" }` for a valid token whose user is missing, deactivated, or whose `sub` is unusable.
- [ ] Protected endpoints return `401` without a valid bearer token; the fallback authorization policy makes new endpoints protected by default.
- [ ] JWT claims are `sub`/`email`/`name`/`jti` with `MapInboundClaims = false` and `RoleClaimType = "role"` declared, so Story 03 can add `role`/`permissions` additively with no breaking change; `sub` is read only through `ClaimsPrincipal.GetUserId()`.
- [ ] The `User` entity carries only the fields login needs, with the documented extension points intact for Story 02, and email normalization is centralized in one reusable helper.
- [ ] Login happens **exactly once per submit**, via `LoginPage → AuthContext.login() → authApi.login() → API`, with no follow-up `me()` call and no direct `authApi` import in `LoginPage`.
- [ ] There is **no circular dependency** between `http.ts` and `AuthContext`: both depend only on `tokenStorage.ts`, and no callback is registered back into the axios module.
- [ ] `AuthContext` exposes a `loading` status so a page refresh with a valid token does not bounce the user to `/login`, and its hydration effect calls `me()` once even under React 19 StrictMode.
- [ ] Passwords are hashed with `PasswordHasher<User>`; no endpoint returns `passwordHash`; no log line contains a password, a hash, or a raw token.
- [ ] `Jwt:SigningKey` is validated at startup (`ValidateOnStart`, ≥ 32 UTF-8 bytes) and sourced from configuration, never hard-coded.
- [ ] CORS allows the frontend origin with `Authorization`/`Content-Type` headers and **without** `AllowCredentials()`; `UseCors` precedes `UseAuthentication`.
- [ ] Diagnostics endpoints live under `/api/diagnostics`, are documented as smoke-test-only, and are called by no frontend feature code.
- [ ] Persistence is **SQL Server** through `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer`. A case-insensitive search of `backend/` for `sqlite`, `UseSqlite`, and `EntityFrameworkCore.InMemory` finds nothing — in source, `.csproj` files, and tests alike.
- [ ] The connection string is read from `ConnectionStrings:Default` and never hard-coded; dev points at LocalDB `CustomerSupportCrmDev`, each integration-test class creates its own uniquely named database and drops it on teardown, and `sqlcmd -S "(localdb)\MSSQLLocalDB" -Q "SELECT name FROM sys.databases"` shows no `CrmAuthTests_*` database left behind after `dotnet test`.
- [ ] The integration-test host runs under the `Testing` environment, so the app's Development-only migrate-and-seed block does not inject the seed admin into test databases.
- [ ] Schema is created by the `InitialCreate` **migration** (not `EnsureCreated`); auto-migrate and seeding run in `Development` only; the seeder is idempotent and warns instead of throwing when unconfigured.
- [ ] The dev seed account is `admin@local.test` (RFC 6761 reserved TLD), used consistently across config, README, tests, and verification steps.
- [ ] Backend and frontend test suites and the frontend typecheck all pass locally.
- [ ] Out-of-scope items (user management, roles/permissions enforcement beyond `Authenticated`, departments/branches, audit logs, branding, MFA, password reset, registration, customer-portal auth, refresh tokens) are **not** implemented.
